extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, and applicants evaluating patent subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the Alice/Mayo two-part eligibility framework to determine whether claimed subject matter is patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101, including identification of judicial exceptions and whether claims add a sufficient inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter). (Step 1: YES/NO)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Method claims are processes; system claims can be machines. If claim is not in a statutory category, it fails Step 1. (Representative analyses: method claim -> process; system claim -> machine.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: Directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas). (Step 2A: YES/NO)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of abstract ideas identified by courts include mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity (e.g., intermediated settlement, hedging, contractual relationships, managing games), and mental processes. The mere presence of an exception does not automatically render a claim ineligible; this is a threshold determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: 'Significantly more' / inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether any element or combination of elements ensures the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception (i.e., whether there is an inventive concept). (Step 2B: YES/NO)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether claim elements add meaningful limitations beyond the abstract idea (e.g., improvements to computer or other technology, unconventional components, specific application). Generic computer implementation, routine data-gathering, or limiting to a field of use typically do not supply 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Using generic computer components to implement an abstract idea does not transform the idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: creating and maintaining 'shadow' accounts (electronic recordkeeping), obtaining data, adjusting account balances, issuing automated instructions—these are well-understood, routine, conventional computer functions. Claims that merely require a generic computer to perform these functions fail Step 2B (see Alice intermediated settlement analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer or other technology can supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that purports to improve the functioning of the computer itself, or to improve another technology or technical field, can provide the necessary inventive concept to make an otherwise abstract idea patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims that produce functional and palpable applications or specific technological improvements (e.g., improved halftoning algorithms that improve image quality, application of a mathematical formula to configure hardware such as an antenna) were found eligible (Research Corp.; Mackay Radio; DDR Holdings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing human activity / fundamental economic practices are abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite longstanding commercial practices or methods of organizing human activity are likely to be characterized as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: intermediated settlement, hedging/consumption risk management, contractual guaranty services, managing bingo games—these concepts are organizing human activity/fundamental economic practices and were treated as abstract ideas in case analyses (Alice, Bilski, buySAFE, Planet Bingo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts and algorithms are abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are essentially mathematical procedures, formulas, or algorithms (including converting representations or organizing numerical data) are abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: BCD-to-binary conversion (Benson), generalized mathematical calculations (SiRF discussed mathematical concepts underlying GPS position calculation), combining data sets via mathematical correlations (Digitech). Such claims require additional limiting inventive concept to be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tying to a specific machine or meaningful limitation can support eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Including a specific machine or device that is essential to the claim and plays a significant part in permitting the claimed method to be performed can meaningfully limit claim scope and support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Presence of a GPS receiver in SiRF was interpreted to place a meaningful limit on the claim because the receiver was essential to perform the method; that contributed to eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a formula to a particular device/configuration may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that practically applies a mathematical formula to configure or operate concrete hardware may be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mackay Radio antenna claim utilized a mathematical formula to arrange antenna wires and was found eligible because it practically applied the formula to configure a particular antenna apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-gathering and pre-solution activity are insignificant
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps that merely gather data or constitute pre-solution activity are generally considered insignificant for purposes of supplying an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Consulting and updating an activity log, restricting public access, or other data-gathering/recordkeeping steps were characterized as insignificant in Ultramercial and do not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting to a particular technological environment is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Restricting an abstract idea to a particular technological environment (e.g., 'on the Internet' or 'online') generally does not render the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Limiting to online transactions or the Internet (buySAFE, Ultramercial) was held insufficient because it is merely a field-of-use limitation and does not supply a non-conventional inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that effect a practical technological improvement can be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that produce a concrete technological improvement or solve a technological problem in a non-generic way can be patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Research Corp. halftoning improved the generated halftoned image (practical application in computer technology); DDR Holdings claims addressing a specific Internet-centric problem were found to supply sufficiently inventive concepts under Alice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting mental steps performed by or with a computer are likely abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that essentially recite familiar mental steps (even if performed by a computer) tend to be characterized as abstract and therefore ineligible absent additional inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: SmartGene claims describing comparing new and stored information and using rules to select medical options were viewed as familiar mental steps and found ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding a 'computer-aided' limitation without more is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely adding that an abstract idea is 'computer-aided' or carried out by conventional computer components does not render the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dealertrack — reducing claim to receiving data, selectively forwarding, and returning decisions; calling this 'computer-aided' did not supply an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing information into a new form needs a specific practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes that merely organize or manipulate information (e.g., combining data sets) are abstract unless the claim ties that organization to a specific structure, machine, or practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Digitech—combining two data sets into a device profile was treated as an abstract process of organizing information because the claim was not tied to a specific image processor or concrete application of the profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine, conventional activity recited at a high level fails to supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: If claimed steps are conventional and specified only at a high level of generality, they do not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ultramercial and buySAFE emphasized that generic, routine activities (even ordered combinations) recited at a high level fail Step 2B. Courts examine whether claim limitations are routine and conventional in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing to a particular type of relationship may not cure abstractness
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely narrowing an abstract idea to a particular type of relationship or particular form of agreement does not necessarily make it non-abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: buySAFE dependent claim narrowing the guaranty to a surety bond, insurance policy, etc., did not change the analysis because it did not remove the abstract nature of creating a contractual guaranty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting to a field of use or adding token post-solution components is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting an abstract idea to a field of use or adding post-solution activity that is token or conventional does not render the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bilski dependent claims and other cases where field-of-use and post-solution components were added did not make the claims patentable; courts require more than token limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of the abstract idea may vary; consider claim as a whole and ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may characterize the abstract idea in different ways; examiners should consider the claim as a whole and whether the ordered combination of elements supplies an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: DDR Holdings discussed multiple possible characterizations of the abstract idea and concluded that, under any reasonable characterization, the claims satisfied step two by reciting a non-conventional solution. Examiners should assess both individual limitations and their ordered combination.
